title: Is Oxford University older than the Aztec Empire?
description:
Is Oxford University older than the Aztec Empire? Not close. Oxford had scholars in residence for over three centuries before the Aztec Empire existed at all.

The University's own recorded history: there is no clear founding date, but teaching existed at Oxford in some form by this year.

They didn't reach the Valley of Mexico and found Tenochtitlan, their future capital, until around 1325. That's already 229 years after Oxford had scholars in residence.

In 1428, after a succession crisis tore apart the region's dominant city, Tenochtitlan's ruler Itzcoatl forged a coup with two smaller cities. That alliance of Tenochtitlan, Texcoco and Tlacopan, known as the Triple Alliance, is what historians call the Aztec Empire.

The gap between Oxford's earliest recorded teaching and the empire most people assume is the older of the two.

Sources:
- https://www.ox.ac.uk/about/the-university/history: read in full. Official University of Oxford history page. Establishes: 'There is no clear date of foundation but teaching existed at Oxford in some form in 1096,' the University's own earliest-recorded-teaching date, well ahead of its listed 1167, 1188 and 1214 milestones.
- https://www.history.com/articles/aztec-empire-triple-alliance: read in full. Article by Dave Roos for HISTORY, drawing on historian Camilla Townsend (Rutgers University, author of Fifth Sun). Establishes that the Mexica people reached the Valley of Mexico and founded Tenochtitlan around 1325 on an island site nobody else wanted; that the ruler of the dominant city Azcapotzalco died in 1426, triggering a succession crisis; and that Tenochtitlan's leader Itzcoatl used the resulting chaos to forge a coup alliance with the smaller cities of Texcoco and Tlacopan, creating the Triple Alliance that historians call the Aztec Empire, which then held power 'for just shy of 100 years (1420s to 1521)' before the Spanish conquest.
